title: JavaScript → TypeScript → React
description: Learn JavaScript and TypeScript, then build React features with tested state updates, asynchronous loading and local persistence.
prerequisites: No React experience required. Be comfortable creating folders and editing text files.
Work through JavaScript lessons before the React sections. Familiarity with HTML is useful but introduced here.
outcomes: Model information with JavaScript arrays and objects.
Use TypeScript to describe values and handle optional data.
Build components, forms and state transitions without mutating previous state.
Explain loading, error and empty states, then test a small tracker.
setup: JavaScript console examples run in a browser developer console or Node.js. Never paste untrusted code into a signed-in website's console.
For React lessons, create a separate practice project using the official React build-from-scratch guide and a current supported Node.js version that meets your chosen tool's requirements.

A learning-only Vite setup: npm create vite@latest notebook-practice -- --template react-ts; cd notebook-practice; npm install; npm run dev. These commands download tools; this notebook does not run them.

Replace src/App.tsx with the downloadable example for the capstone. Keep the generated main.tsx. Remove starter App.css imports if experimenting with appearance. Run npm run build to type-check/build.
The downloadable kit now includes a pinned runnable Vite/Vitest project: npm ci, npm test, npm run build, npm run dev from the extracted folder root.
nextSteps: Study your chosen production framework's server rendering, caching and deployment model.
Implement and test the advanced project against a real authenticated API.
Continue with design systems, internationalization and production observability.

lessons.title: 1. The browser, HTML and JavaScript
lessons.takeaway: HTML gives meaning, CSS controls presentation and JavaScript changes behavior.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A browser turns a document into an interactive page. A button has a role, focus behavior and keyboard activation that a clickable div does not automatically provide. Start with meaningful elements before styling.

The tiny example is a complete HTML fragment. Its label tells a user what the input means. A React application still produces ordinary browser elements; React is not a replacement for HTML or accessibility.
sections.example:
<label for="topic">Topic</label>
<input id="topic" name="topic" />
<button type="button">Add topic</button>

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: A placeholder disappears when typing and is not a substitute for a persistent label. Avoid using color alone to indicate errors.

exercise.prompt: Write markup for a study-minutes number input with a label and a Save button.
exercise.solution:
<label for="minutes">Study minutes</label>
<input id="minutes" type="number" min="0" />
<button type="button">Save</button>
checks: Clicking the label focuses the input.
Tab reaches the input and button.
This markup does not save anything until behavior is added.

quiz.question: Which element already supports keyboard activation?
options: A span with a click handler
quiz.explanation: Native controls provide useful behavior and semantics. Styling a generic element does not add them.

lessons.title: 2. Values, equality and conversion
lessons.takeaway: Convert at boundaries; do not rely on accidental coercion.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Input values arrive as strings even when they look numeric. Convert the text, then validate the result. Number('') is zero, so check for blank input before conversion.

const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not freeze an object. Use strict equality to compare values without automatic type conversion. A missing value may be undefined; intentional absence often uses null.

sections.title: Enough syntax to write the first validator
paragraphs: function parseMinutes(raw) declares an operation with an input named raw. Braces delimit its body. return sends a value back and ends that call; console.log displays a value instead. if (condition) runs its following statement only when the condition is true.

The expression condition ? first : second chooses one value. && requires both conditions to hold and skips its right side when the left is false. Read Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 0 ? n : null as: return n only when it is a nonnegative integer, otherwise return null. The later functions lesson expands this into reusable transformations.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Treating every falsy value as missing rejects valid zero. Check for missing input separately from zero.

sections.title: Run a small progression
paragraphs: Run practice/javascript-steps.js with Node. Predict conversion results, edit one assertion to observe a failure, then restore it. Continue through array transformation, an immutable update and rejected async work before working with component state.

sections.title: Follow conversion before choosing a fallback
paragraphs: An HTML number input still exposes text through its value property. Number("") becomes zero, which can turn an unanswered field into a legitimate zero-minute session. First distinguish missing text from an entered zero, then convert, check finiteness and the allowed range. Similarly, value || 20 replaces a valid zero; value ?? 20 replaces only null and undefined.

The focused foundation-data.ts lab accepts already-decoded numeric data. Its parser rejects the string "20" rather than converting it to a number. A form adapter can convert entered text, while the shared parser keeps its domain contract unambiguous. TypeScript annotations alone do not convert strings arriving at runtime.

exercise.prompt: Write parseMinutes(raw) that returns null for blanks, negatives or non-integers.
checks: Zero is accepted.
Blank and fractional input are rejected.
Use null explicitly rather than testing result with !result.

quiz.question: What is Number('')?
quiz.explanation: An empty string converts to zero; validate blank input before converting.

lessons.title: 3. Arrays, objects and transformations
lessons.takeaway: Keep source records separate from derived views.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: An array is an ordered collection. An object groups named properties for one record. map transforms every element, filter selects elements and reduce combines them into one value.
A learning tracker can store records once and derive completed titles or totals when needed. A derived array need not be another mutable source of truth.

sections.title: Read callbacks one element at a time
paragraphs: x => x.done is a small function whose input is one record and whose result is its done field. filter calls it for each record and keeps records producing true. map calls its function for each retained record and collects the returned values. Neither operation deep-copies the objects.

reduce((sum, x) => sum + x.minutes, 0) starts sum at 0 and replaces it with the returned value after each item. With completed minutes 20 and 15, the accumulator becomes 20 then 35. An empty array leaves the initial 0 unchanged.

The spread form [...items] creates a new array containing the same items. In the next lesson, {...row, done: true} copies an object's fields and replaces done. Nested objects still remain shared; copy the particular nested object when changing it.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: sort mutates an array. Use [...items].sort(...) when the original order must remain intact. A shallow copy still shares nested objects.

exercise.prompt: Return total minutes for completed records only.
checks: The result is 35.
An empty array returns 0.
The input records remain unchanged.

quiz.question: Which operation selects a subset?
quiz.explanation: filter keeps matching elements. map transforms elements without changing the count.

lessons.title: 4. Functions and predictable behavior
lessons.takeaway: A small pure function is easier to explain and test.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A function receives inputs and returns an output. A pure function depends only on its inputs and does not change external state. Logging and network calls are side effects; they are useful, but keep them at clear boundaries.
Arrow functions are concise syntax, not a separate execution model. A function passed as an argument can be called later; calling it immediately passes its result instead.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Returning nothing yields undefined. In an arrow function with braces, write return explicitly.

sections.title: Trace references through an update
paragraphs: Copying an array with [...rows] copies its container, not every object inside it. If next[0].done = true, both containers still point to the same first object. The old state has now changed too. Instead, create a new object for the changed row and retain unchanged rows. This makes the ownership decision explicit before you use the code in React.

Complete and toggle are different operations. Repeating complete should leave a row completed; repeating toggle changes it back. Choose the operation from the user intent and retry behavior. The focused lab tests repeated completion and a missing ID, so a convenient toggle implementation cannot silently replace the contract.

exercise.prompt: Implement toggleById(rows, id) without changing rows or its objects.
checks: The selected item flips.
An unknown ID leaves all values unchanged.
The original selected object is not mutated.

quiz.question: What should an event handler receive?
options: Always the result of calling a function now
quiz.explanation: Passing a function defers work until the event occurs.

lessons.title: 5. Promises and API boundaries
lessons.takeaway: An asynchronous result needs success, failure and loading behavior.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A Promise represents eventual completion or failure. await pauses the current async function, not the whole browser. Use try/catch to handle rejections and decide what the user should see.
fetch resolves for many HTTP errors, including 404; inspect response.ok. JSON parsing is not schema validation. Treat external data as untrusted and check its shape before using it.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Launching dependent requests simultaneously can use data that is not ready. Conversely, unrelated requests can often run together with Promise.all; one rejection rejects that combined promise.

sections.title: Two requests can finish in reverse order
paragraphs: Imagine searching P, then Python. The P request may return last. Await inside each request orders that request's steps, but does not order independent calls. Assign a request number when starting; apply a result only if it still belongs to the current request. Cancellation can reduce wasted work, while the identity check determines which result may update the view.

Check which request produced an error, too. An old request must not replace a newer success with an error message. Apply the identity check to both success and failure paths, and clear the loading state only for the current request. The later race-safe loading lesson and its existing tests implement this fuller UI boundary.

exercise.prompt: Handle a simulated rejection and return an empty list only after explicitly recording the error.
checks: The rejection is handled.
The fallback is deliberate, not a silent success.
In a UI, display an error and retry option rather than disguising failure as an empty dataset.

quiz.question: Does fetch automatically reject on HTTP 404?
quiz.explanation: Check response.ok or status; an HTTP response can resolve the promise even when its status is an error.

lessons.title: 6. TypeScript and narrowing
lessons.takeaway: Types check assumptions during development; validate external data at runtime.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: TypeScript adds a static type checker to JavaScript. A union such as string | null describes alternatives. A conditional can narrow that union before an operation is used.
An interface describes an expected shape, but it does not inspect a network response. Casting with as does not make unknown data valid. Start with unknown at external boundaries and check it.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: any disables useful checking. Prefer a specific type or unknown with narrowing when the shape is not yet established.

sections.title: Narrow unknown data step by step
paragraphs: Treat parsed JSON as unknown. Check that it is a non-null object and not an array, then inspect fields. In foundation-data.ts, a result with ok: true carries a validated Session; ok: false carries an error string. Testing result.ok lets TypeScript narrow the union before you access value. The type follows the runtime check.

A cast such as JSON.parse(text) as Session skips all those checks. It can compile while minutes is "twenty". The lab rejects malformed values, preserves zero, trims identity text into a fresh value, and leaves the caller's object unchanged. Readonly helps prevent accidental writes in typed code, but is not a runtime freeze or an authorization rule.

sections.title: Prepare a versioned importer in small steps
paragraphs: The foundation project returns a summary from a function; a React upload screen comes later. First parse text with JSON.parse inside try/catch, then narrow the resulting unknown. Check version before reading lessons. Reject arrays where an object is expected, and inspect each lesson's id, title and done before deriving a count.

Use a fresh Set to track IDs: seen.has(id) detects a duplicate and seen.add(id) records a new ID. For {version:1, lessons:[{id:"a", title:"Types", done:false}]}, the summary is total 1, complete 0. Empty lessons gives 0 and 0. The same ID twice must fail, even if its titles differ. Check these independently before looking at decodeSaved.

exercise.prompt: Accept unknown and return a nonnegative integer or null.
checks: String '3' is not accepted as a number.
Negative, fractional and NaN values return null.
No unsafe assertion is needed.

quiz.question: Does an interface validate JSON?
quiz.explanation: Types are not runtime validators; a server can return data that violates your declared type.

lessons.title: 7. Components, props and lists
lessons.takeaway: Pass data down and keep each component's responsibility clear.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A component renders one part of the interface from its inputs. Props are supplied by its parent. Begin with a static screen so the component boundaries are understandable before adding behavior.

Use stable record IDs for list keys. The key helps React match elements between renders; it is not an ordinary prop automatically received by the child. In the snippet, the parent passes title separately.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Array indexes are fragile keys when records can be inserted, deleted or reordered. Do not generate new random keys on every render.

exercise.prompt: Extend LessonRow to display a completed marker using a done prop.
checks: Complete and To do are visible text.
Props are not modified by the component.
The parent supplies the status.

quiz.question: Which key is most appropriate for reorderable records?
options: A new random number every render
quiz.explanation: A stable identity lets React match the same record through list changes.

lessons.title: 8. Events, state and immutable updates
lessons.takeaway: State is a snapshot; request the next state instead of mutating the current one.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: React state retains information between renders. A setter requests another render. The current event handler still sees the snapshot from the render that created it.

When an update depends on previous state, a functional updater communicates that dependency. Create new arrays and changed objects so the update is explicit. Keep calculated totals derived from the current records.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Directly changing an object in state does not request a render. Also avoid storing both records and a separately maintained completed count when the count can be derived.

sections.title: Test the transition before wiring a component
paragraphs: The focused lab exposes transition(rows, action) as an ordinary TypeScript function. With rows a and b, completing a returns a changed copy of a and keeps b. The test freezes the input to expose mutation immediately. You can inspect the output without rendering a component or understanding a testing library for DOM events.

Build a component that calls setRows(previous => transition(previous, action)) once the transition is understood. Derived totals should be calculated from rows rather than maintained in a second independent state variable. A later component test still matters: passing transition tests does not prove that the button dispatches the right ID.

exercise.prompt: Write the state update to toggle record id 'types'.
checks: The selected object is copied.
Unchanged records retain their values.
A second toggle returns to the original status.

quiz.question: What does a state setter do?
options: Mutates the current local variable immediately
Requests a future render with updated state
quiz.explanation: The current render's snapshot remains unchanged; a new render receives the next state.

frames.label: Render one
frames.explanation: The handler closes over this render's snapshot.

frames.label: User clicks
frames.explanation: The updater computes the next count. The current snapshot is still zero.

frames.label: Render two
frames.explanation: React renders using the next state and updates the visible result.

lessons.title: 9. Forms, validation and derived views
lessons.takeaway: Store user input; derive filtered output from it.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A controlled input receives its value from state and reports changes through an event handler. Keep the input's accessible label visible. A form can handle submission from both a button and the Enter key.
Search results are derived from records plus the search query. There is no need to copy them into another state variable. Validate on submit, and explain errors in text near the field.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: This is a component fragment, not a full file. Hooks must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not inside a conditional.

exercise.prompt: Describe and implement a trimmed title validator.
checks: Whitespace-only input fails.
A valid title is trimmed.
Show a visible error; do not rely on an alert or red border alone.
Run npm test in the downloaded project. Find the relevant assertion in ui.test.tsx, temporarily remove the behavior it checks, and confirm that the test fails. Restore the behavior afterward.

quiz.question: Should filtered results usually be stored separately?
options: No, calculate them from records and query
quiz.explanation: A derived value avoids synchronizing duplicate state.

lessons.title: 10. Effects and external systems
lessons.takeaway: Use Effects to synchronize external systems, not to calculate ordinary derived values.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: An Effect can connect a component to something outside rendering, such as browser storage or a subscription. Cleanup releases resources or prevents obsolete work from affecting the current screen.

Fetching data in an Effect needs loading and error handling plus protection from stale results. Frameworks and data libraries can manage these concerns. Do not suppress dependencies just to stop an Effect from running.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: An Effect may be set up and cleaned up extra times in development Strict Mode. Design correct cleanup instead of relying on a single execution.

exercise.prompt: Choose whether a completed count needs an Effect, then implement it.
exercise.solution:
const completedCount = lessons.filter(row => row.done).length;
// Derived during rendering; no Effect or separate count state required.
checks: Changing lessons changes the count on the next render.
No extra synchronization step exists.
Use Effects only for actual external synchronization.

quiz.question: Which operation needs no Effect?
options: Subscribing to an external event source
quiz.explanation: Pure calculations can run during rendering.

lessons.title: 11. Build and test a learning tracker
lessons.takeaway: Finish a small complete feature before adding a larger architecture.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Download App.tsx and run it in the React TypeScript project from setup. It has a search input, stable IDs, toggles and a derived completion count. It keeps data in memory so you can study state changes before adding storage.

Test behavior through the screen: keyboard focus, blank search, mixed-case search, toggling, and an empty result. Then change one requirement at a time. Treat loading, failure and server validation as separate work when adding an API.
sections.example:
Acceptance scenario:
1. Initial count: 0 of 3 complete.
2. Mark Types complete: 1 of 3 complete.
3. Search STATE: one record remains visible.
4. Clear search: Types remains complete.
5. Refresh: in-memory state resets.

sections.title: Pitfalls
paragraphs: Do not claim persistence just because a value survives changing a filter. This example resets after a page reload and has no backend.

exercise.prompt: Add a Show incomplete only checkbox and combine it with text filtering.
checks: Both filters apply together.
The total completion count still reflects all records.
An empty list has an explanatory message.

quiz.question: What must be added for progress across devices?
options: A persistence/synchronization design, usually involving a backend
quiz.explanation: Memory state is local to a running page. Cross-device data needs storage, identity and synchronization decisions.

lessons.title: Modules, closures and the event loop
lessons.takeaway: A closure retains access to its lexical environment; scheduling decides when a callback observes it.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: Split a growing program by responsibility. A named export gives an explicit module interface. A closure can hide mutable state, but hidden state can also make tests depend on call order. Promise callbacks run after the current synchronous work completes; a zero-delay timer is not an instruction to run immediately.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The two counters retain independent value variables, producing 1, 2, 1. The promise callback runs after synchronous code, so the log order is A, C, B.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Each call to makeCounter creates a distinct environment. A React handler similarly belongs to a render snapshot; long-lived callbacks may retain older values. Treat module-level mutable state as a shared singleton and avoid using it for independent users' data.

exercise.prompt: Write a multiplier factory and show that two instances do not interfere.
checks: Explain lexical capture rather than saying values are copied automatically.
Synchronous logs precede Promise callbacks.
Separate module exports from per-instance state.

quiz.question: Which log order does the example produce?
quiz.explanation: Promise reactions wait until the current synchronous work has finished.

lessons.title: Discriminated unions and validated boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Represent valid states so that impossible combinations are difficult to express.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: Two booleans loading and failed can produce confusing combinations. A discriminated union uses one tag to distinguish loading, success and failure. Render by the tag, and TypeScript narrows the remaining fields. Runtime data must still be checked before constructing the success state.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The TypeScript function narrows Remote by status. Only the success branch reads data; an empty successful array is described as 0 lessons.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A cast merely changes what the checker assumes. Prefer decoding unknown into a validated domain object. Decide how to handle extra fields, invalid IDs, duplicates and payload size. Do not log entire sensitive responses just to debug a validation failure.

exercise.prompt: Define a save-state union that distinguishes idle, saving and failed with a message.
exercise.solution:
type SaveState = {kind:"idle"} | {kind:"saving"} | {kind:"failed"; message:string};
function isBusy(state: SaveState) { return state.kind === "saving"; }
checks: Only failed has a message.
A success state never silently contains invalid external data.
Explain a runtime test the compiler cannot perform.

quiz.question: Does a type assertion validate a server response?
quiz.explanation: Type assertions are erased; validation must execute at runtime.

lessons.title: Reducers, actions and domain invariants
lessons.takeaway: Centralize state transitions when related updates must remain consistent.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: A reducer receives previous state and an action and returns next state. Keep it pure: no network calls, random IDs or storage writes inside it. Generate an ID in the event handler and pass it in an action. The reducer can reject duplicate IDs or invalid titles according to a documented contract.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The reducer returns new arrays for toggle and remove; toggle also copies the matching row. The final comment shows how a component connects this function to useReducer.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A reducer does not make a state machine correct by itself. Write invariants such as unique IDs and nonblank titles, then test every action against them. Unknown IDs can be no-ops; document and test that choice.

exercise.prompt: Test that toggling twice restores values without modifying the original input.
checks: Original objects remain unchanged.
Unknown ID behavior is specified.
IDs are generated outside the reducer.

quiz.question: Where should a network save happen?
options: In an effect/event boundary outside the reducer
quiz.explanation: A reducer should remain deterministic and free of side effects.

lessons.title: Context, custom Hooks and ownership
lessons.takeaway: When a custom Hook calls useState, each invocation gets its own state. Lift state to a shared owner when components need the same value.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: A custom Hook packages reusable stateful behavior. Two components calling the same Hook normally receive separate state. Context can distribute a shared value from an ancestor, but it is not a replacement for deciding who owns that value.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: This Hook fragment gives each invocation its own state. The functional update flips the current value; sharing the Hook implementation does not couple its callers.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Put local form input near the component using it. Put shared records at the nearest suitable shared owner. A context value change updates consumers; splitting unrelated contexts may help, but measure before adding indirection. Hooks must obey the top-level calling rules.

exercise.prompt: Describe ownership for a search box, a selected lesson and shared lesson records.
exercise.solution:
Search draft: local to the search feature unless the URL must preserve it.
Selected lesson: route/URL state when deep linking matters.
Lesson records: shared owner or data cache.
Derived filtered records: calculate from records and search; do not store a duplicate.
checks: Explain which values should survive navigation.
Avoid a global context for every keystroke.
Test two independent instances of the same Hook.

quiz.question: Do two calls to useToggle share one boolean?
options: No, each call has its own state
quiz.explanation: Hooks reuse logic; state belongs to each mounted call location.

lessons.title: Component identity and form resets
lessons.takeaway: State belongs to a component's position and identity in the rendered tree.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: Switching a prop does not necessarily reset local state. An editor initialized from props may still contain the previous record's draft when a different record is selected. Decide whether to preserve drafts, reset on identity change, or store drafts by record ID.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: In this parent fragment, changing selectedLesson.id changes the key and remounts the editor. Local state resets, including any draft not saved elsewhere.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A key reset is a product decision. Warn or preserve work where appropriate; do not use random keys to force refresh. Lifting state lets you preserve a draft across remounts but increases coordination. Test both switching records and re-rendering the same record.

exercise.prompt: Write acceptance checks for switching between two editable lesson records.
exercise.solution:
1. Edit A without saving.
2. Select B: B must not show A’s title.
3. Return to A: either restored draft or explicit reset, matching the chosen policy.
4. A normal rerender of A must not unexpectedly erase its draft.
checks: The draft policy is stated.
Stable keys reflect record identity.
Validation errors reset or persist according to the same policy.

quiz.question: What does changing a component's key generally do?
options: Preserves the old component state by default
Gives it a new identity and resets local state
quiz.explanation: A different key changes the identity React uses to preserve state.

lessons.title: Race-safe asynchronous screens
lessons.takeaway: Cancellation and stale-result protection keep old requests from overwriting newer intent.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: If a user selects A and then B, A's slower response may arrive last. Without a guard, the screen can show A while the heading says B. An AbortController can cancel a fetch, while a cleanup flag prevents obsolete callbacks from committing state.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: This Effect fragment needs itemId, setView and decode from its component. Cleanup both aborts the request and marks the result inactive, preventing an obsolete response from updating the view.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: This fragment assumes decode and setView are stable or otherwise correctly included in dependencies. A data-fetching library/framework may supply caching, invalidation and deduplication. A response cache key must include all inputs affecting the result. Retrying a write is more consequential than retrying a read.

exercise.prompt: Design a deterministic test with controllable promises for A and B.
exercise.solution:
Start A, then switch to B.
Resolve B first with title B.
Resolve A afterward with title A.
Assert the visible selected record remains B.
Also test a rejected B, unmount during load and a malformed successful response.
checks: A stale success cannot overwrite B.
Cleanup does not show an error for intentional cancellation.
Loading, error, empty and success are distinct.
Run npm test in the downloaded project. Find the relevant assertion in ui.test.tsx, temporarily remove the behavior it checks, and confirm that the test fails. Restore the behavior afterward.

quiz.question: A starts, selection changes to B, B resolves, then A resolves. An adapter ignores AbortSignal. What preserves B?
options: AbortController alone guarantees no promise callback can run
A cleanup flag/request identity check ignores the superseded result
Calling setState for every response in arrival order
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative. Cleanup must also prevent an obsolete callback from committing state when the adapter ignores abort.

lessons.title: URLs, navigation and shareable state
lessons.takeaway: Navigation state belongs in a URL when users need to bookmark or share it.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: A selected lesson, search query or page number may need to survive refresh and Back. A local state variable alone does not provide that behavior. Production routers handle route matching and history integration; understand the browser model before choosing abstractions.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The URL parser reads q and validates page as a positive integer, falling back to 1. pushState changes browser history without emitting popstate itself.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Treat URL parameters as untrusted input. Decide which changes push a new history entry and which replace the current one. A deployed SPA also needs deep-link fallback handling unless it uses hash routes. Focus and document titles must update coherently after navigation.

exercise.prompt: Specify expected Back-button behavior for filtering and selecting a lesson.
exercise.solution:
Use replace for rapidly edited search drafts if every keystroke should not become a history entry.
Use push for selecting another lesson.
On Back, restore route state from the URL, update the screen and focus the main heading.
Test a direct deep link and a refresh at that URL.
checks: Bad page values fall back safely.
The URL and screen cannot disagree.
Test actual browser history rather than only a component mock.
Run npm test in the downloaded project. Find the relevant assertion in ui.test.tsx, temporarily remove the behavior it checks, and confirm that the test fails. Restore the behavior afterward.

quiz.question: A button calls history.pushState to select State. No popstate event arrives. What should the app do?
options: Wait for popstate because pushState always emits it synchronously
Update selection in the click handler and listen for popstate for history traversal
Reload the whole page after every selection
quiz.explanation: pushState changes the URL/history without emitting popstate. Update local selection directly; Back/Forward use the popstate listener.

lessons.title: Tests that verify behavior
lessons.takeaway: Test domain logic, component interactions and browser journeys at appropriate boundaries.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: A reducer unit test can cover invariants cheaply. A component test checks accessible labels, actions and rendered outcomes. A browser test covers integration such as navigation and storage. A snapshot alone rarely proves that a feature works.

The kit supplies ui.test.tsx, vite.config.ts and locked dependencies. npm test executes five component regressions plus domain checks; the Back/Forward test exercises jsdom history, while a browser refresh/keyboard review remains separate evidence.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The kit supplies the imports and test environment for this fragment. The test finds controls by accessible role and name, completes the Types lesson, and checks visible progress.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Queries by role and accessible name tend to reflect real user interaction. Avoid tests coupled to internal state variable names or CSS selectors when a semantic query is possible. Use controllable asynchronous fixtures instead of arbitrary sleeps.

exercise.prompt: Create a test matrix for the tracker's add/remove/filter behavior.
exercise.solution:
Unit: blank title, duplicate ID, unknown toggle, input immutability.
Component: labeled input, Enter submission, visible validation error, empty filter result.
Browser: refresh policy, keyboard-only operation, URL Back/Forward if routing is added.
Regression: reproduce one real bug with the smallest meaningful test.
checks: Each test has an observable expected result.
At least one negative case per boundary.
Do not mark a test passed merely because it did not throw during setup.
Run npm test in the downloaded project. Find the relevant assertion in ui.test.tsx, temporarily remove the behavior it checks, and confirm that the test fails. Restore the behavior afterward.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest test of an Add button?
options: Activating it creates the expected visible record
quiz.explanation: The second checks user-visible behavior.

lessons.title: Error boundaries and security boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Recoverable UI failures and access-control decisions are different responsibilities.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: An Error Boundary can show a fallback for rendering errors in its descendants. It does not automatically handle every event-handler or asynchronous error, so those paths still need explicit handling. Place boundaries around features that can fail independently.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: JSX renders externalTitle as text. Rendering it as untrusted HTML would change the security boundary; server authorization is still required for protected operations.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: React's ordinary text rendering escapes text, but that does not make arbitrary URLs, HTML injection or all third-party code safe. Validate destinations and data. Do not ship API secrets in client bundles. A hidden admin button cannot prevent someone sending the underlying request.

exercise.prompt: Threat-model a lesson editor with public read and owner-only write.
exercise.solution:
Server verifies identity and ownership on every write.
Client validates for usability; server validates authoritatively.
Render titles as text; sanitize only if explicitly supporting rich HTML.
Avoid logging tokens or full sensitive payloads.
Handle expired sessions without silently losing a local draft.
checks: Describe what an attacker can bypass in the UI.
Distinguish rendering failures from rejected API calls.
Test unauthorized writes at the server boundary.

quiz.question: Is hiding a Delete button sufficient authorization?
quiz.explanation: Requests can be sent without using the visible UI.

references.title: React Component: Error Boundaries
references.section: Catching rendering errors with an Error Boundary
references.scope: Primary guidance checked for descendant rendering errors and excluded error paths; not a browser execution claim.

references.title: OWASP XSS prevention
references.scope: Primary guidance checked for framework escape hatches and untrusted HTML/URL boundaries; not a full application security audit.

lessons.title: Measure before optimizing
lessons.takeaway: An optimization should preserve behavior and improve a measured bottleneck.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: A slow interaction may come from rendering, a long calculation, layout or a network waterfall. Record the slow interaction and inspect the appropriate profiler. Memoization trades bookkeeping and memory for potentially avoided work; it is not a correctness mechanism.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: This component fragment caches expensiveFilter by rows and query. Its usefulness depends on measured cost and stable dependencies; a new rows reference invalidates the cache.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: React memo compares props shallowly by default; new object/function identities may still trigger work. A custom comparator can be wrong when it ignores callbacks with captured state. Large lists may need virtualization; it introduces keyboard and accessibility considerations. Compiler-enabled projects can change how much manual memoization is useful.

sections.title: Separate benchmark fixture
paragraphs: The tracker accepts at most 1,000 records. Run practice/performance-fixture.ts for 10,000 synthetic records; do not import that array into the tracker. Compare calculation timing with React Profiler evidence from a real UI interaction before choosing an optimization.

exercise.prompt: Use practice/performance-fixture.ts for a separate 10,000-record synthetic filter. Keep the tracker's 1,000-record validation limit. Record repeated filter and UI Profiler measurements, correctness and device/build.
exercise.solution:
Use a fixed synthetic dataset and the same device/build.
Measure typing-to-update latency and render/calculate time.
Try removing redundant state first.
Compare a memoized filter or deferred presentation only if warranted.
Check result correctness and keyboard behavior after optimization.
checks: Report workload and build mode.
Do not use console timings alone to prove a whole interaction improved.
Remove an optimization if it adds complexity without benefit.

quiz.question: Should useMemo be required for correctness?
quiz.explanation: The result must remain correct if React recomputes it.

lessons.title: Persistence, releases and a production-readiness review
lessons.takeaway: A working local screen still needs a reliable data and delivery contract.

sections.title: Contract
paragraphs: Persistence introduces schema versions, invalid stored data, quota failures and multi-device conflict decisions. A browser-only tracker may use local storage for non-sensitive learning data, but it must handle read/write failures and cannot promise cross-device synchronization.

sections.title: Example
paragraphs: The versioned envelope supports validation and migration of persisted lessons. The release sequence covers build correctness, navigation, keyboard use, failure behavior and operational recovery.
sections.example:
Persistence envelope:
{ "version": 1, "lessons": [{"id":"types","title":"Types","done":false}] }

Release checks:
Type-check → domain tests → UI tests → production build → preview
Deep-link refresh → keyboard flow → error states → monitoring → rollback plan

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Deploying static files does not create a backend. If APIs are added, configure origins, HTTPS, authentication and server-side validation. Keep configuration separate from secrets. Record the user interactions you tested. A successful build alone does not test those interactions.

sections.title: Guided advanced milestones
paragraphs: See practice/README.md and the persistence-bridge.ts and http-loader.ts exercises. Wire migration and storage into a copy of the tracker, then wire a real training API into RemoteLesson. Submit refresh, malformed data, HTTP error, race, authorization and unsaved-draft evidence. The supplied app still uses in-memory data and a local delayed loader until you complete those steps.

exercise.prompt: Build the advanced tracker project and produce an evidence-based release note.
exercise.solution:
Reference architecture:
- tracker-core.ts owns schema validation and pure transitions.
- AdvancedApp.tsx owns form state and dispatches actions.
- Persistence adapter handles versioned decoding and explicit failures.
- Tests cover invalid input, duplicate IDs and immutable updates.
- Add API synchronization only with documented conflict and authorization rules.
Report exactly which checks ran and which deployment assumptions remain.
checks: All required project cases pass.
No secrets in client code.
An incompatible saved version fails clearly.
A rollback preserves or deliberately migrates user data.

quiz.question: Does deploying a SPA make its data available across devices?
options: Only with a designed persistence/synchronization service
quiz.explanation: A hosted interface and shared persistent data are separate systems.

stages.title: Foundations: JavaScript and typed data
stages.description: Practise JavaScript values, browser behavior and runtime validation before adding React state.
exitCriteria: Write small pure functions and test invalid as well as normal input.
Explain strings versus numbers, asynchronous completion and TypeScript's runtime limits.
Use semantic labeled controls and distinguish data from its display.

project.title: Validated study-record importer
project.brief: Convert an unknown JSON payload into a useful summary without trusting type assertions.
requirements: Accept a versioned object containing unique lesson IDs, titles and completion booleans.
Reject malformed JSON, duplicate IDs, blank titles and unsupported versions.
Return a completion summary without modifying caller-owned records.
Write repeatable valid and invalid-input tests.
rubric: Every malformed case produces an explicit failure.
Zero and false are not treated as missing.
Explain where runtime validation ends and static typing begins.
project.solution: Parse into unknown. Check the envelope version and array. Validate each record and use a Set for duplicate IDs. Construct new typed records. Derive counts with filter/reduce. See decodeSaved and tracker-core.test.ts for a reference implementation; attempt your own before opening it.

stages.title: Intermediate: state and feature design
stages.description: Build features with defined state ownership, tested transitions and accessible controls.
exitCriteria: Choose between local state, lifted state, reducers and context.
Implement forms with visible validation and stable list identity.
Test transitions and explain draft-reset policies.

project.title: Editable learning tracker
project.brief: Build a tracker that lets users add, toggle, remove and search records. Keep its data transformations pure and its controls usable with a keyboard.
requirements: Use stable IDs and immutable reducer transitions.
Show blank-title errors and an empty search result.
Keep completion counts derived from all records.
Decide whether changing selection preserves unsaved drafts.
Run domain tests and manually verify Enter, Tab and checkbox behavior.
rubric: No duplicated records or mutation of old state.
Filtering does not lose completion changes.
A failed input cannot appear as a successful update.
Explain the ownership of each state value.
project.solution: Separate tracker-core.ts from AdvancedApp.tsx. Generate IDs in event handlers, validate domain transitions in the reducer, derive filtered rows during rendering and use a labeled form. The downloadable workshop implements these interactions in memory; storage and API synchronization are separate extensions.

stages.title: Selected advanced practice
stages.description: Test asynchronous races, local persistence, security assumptions and performance in a small application.
exitCriteria: Prevent stale requests from overwriting newer intent.
Distinguish render boundaries, async failures and server authorization.
Design versioned persistence and a realistic release test plan.
Measure a slow interaction before choosing an optimization.

project.title: Resilient tracker release
project.brief: Add versioned persistence and recovery to the workshop. Test the release candidate and list the checks that still need a deployed application.
requirements: Add persistence with explicit save/read failure handling and schema version checks.
Implement a controllable API adapter with loading, error and stale-response tests.
Add URL-selected records and verify Back/Forward and direct-link refresh.
Prevent unsaved edits being silently overwritten.
Document server authorization assumptions and keep secrets out of the client.
Provide before/after measurements for one genuine bottleneck or explain why no optimization was justified.
rubric: Delayed response A cannot overwrite newer record B.
Malformed storage remains visible as an error rather than silently trusted data.
Release notes distinguish executed tests from reviewed-only code.
project.solution: Start from the tested domain core. Add storage and API adapters around it, not inside the reducer. Use request cleanup and stale-result guards or a suitable framework data layer. Test adapter failures deterministically. The supplied app is a reference starting point, not a claim that these advanced extensions are already implemented.
